chunks: How a MOSFET works. The question: How does it work?
A MOSFET is a switch where the gate voltage builds a conducting path in the silicon. With the gate off, the source and drain are cut off from each other.
With enough gate voltage, a thin layer under the gate turns into a channel that connects them. The gate never touches that channel. It acts through an electric field.
Picture two ponds separated by dry land, with a flat metal plate hovering over the land.
Charge the plate and the ground beneath it fills with electrons, forming a shallow strip of water that joins the ponds.
The ponds are the source and drain, and the strip is the channel. Remove the charge and the strip dries up. One limit of the picture: the plate adds no water itself.
Its charge only pulls electrons already in the silicon up to the surface.
An NMOS with the gate above threshold and a small V DS.
The positive gate has pushed holes away (orange depletion region of ionized acceptors) and pulled a thin sheet of electrons to the surface (the channel).
Without that sheet, source-body-drain is N-P-N: two back-to-back diodes, so nothing flows.
Channel: the thin conducting layer that forms under the gate. Threshold voltage ( V t ): the gate voltage where the channel forms.
P-type and N-type: silicon treated so that it carries current mainly with positive "holes" or mainly with electrons.
Depletion region: the area where the gate field pushes away the free charges that were there. Inversion: the body surface flipping from P-type to N-type under the gate.
Triode and saturation: resistor-like and constant-current behavior.
Take an N-channel MOSFET with a threshold of about 2 volts.
With the gate at 0 volts, the path from source to drain is N, then P, then N, which is two back-to-back diodes (one-way valves for current facing opposite ways), so no current flows.
Raise the gate to 5 volts and the surface under it flips to N-type. Now there is a continuous path, and a voltage between drain and source drives current through it.
That is the whole idea.
"Take an NMOS: a P-type body with N-type source and drain, and a gate on a thin oxide in between. With no gate voltage, it's two back-to-back diodes, so no current.
A positive gate voltage first pushes holes away, then, past threshold, pulls enough electrons to the surface to form an N-type channel linking source and drain.
V DS drives current through it, and more overdrive means more channel charge and lower resistance. At high V DS the channel pinches off at the drain and the current saturates.
The gate controls everything through the field, with no DC current."
